key_claim: US nonfarm payrolls rose by 29,000 in September 2026 against an average monthly gain of 45,000 over the prior 12 months, with July revised down to -10,000 and unemployment at 4.2%.
frame_summary: Reports a labour market that is hiring very little but not shedding workers: payroll growth near zero, unemployment essentially unchanged, and prior months revised down.

publisher: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: The Economic Outlook and Some Comments on My Policy Communication (Governor Waller)
key_claim: Job creation has averaged 60,000 a month through July 2026, close to what it takes to keep pace with slow labour-force growth, which Governor Waller attributes mostly to much lower net immigration.
frame_summary: Argues the current pace of job creation is roughly adequate for a labour force growing slowly, mainly because of lower immigration, rather than a sign of demand weakness.
verbatim_quote: Job creation, though a bit volatile, has increased this year by an average of 60,000 a month through July.
verbatim_list: close to and probably a bit above estimates of what it takes to keep pace with the slow growth in the labor force
mostly because of much lower net immigration
notes: Central bank governor speech, Tier 1. Quotes confirmed by web fetch 10 October 2026; on-device fetch blocked (proxy 403).

publisher: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
title: An Update on AI and the Economy (Governor Cook)
key_claim: The labour market has stayed resilient through early AI adoption, but recent college graduates face more difficulty finding first jobs, possibly partly because of AI's ability to take on entry-level tasks.
frame_summary: Argues AI has not yet broken the aggregate labour market, while flagging a concentrated entry-level effect worth monitoring.
verbatim_quote: In addition, many recent college graduates are facing more difficulty finding their first jobs.
verbatim_list: This is possibly partly related to AI's ability to take on entry-level tasks.
notes: Central bank governor speech, Tier 1. Supplies the strongest sourced objection (entry-level weakness) in the Counter-Argument. Confirmed by web fetch 10 October 2026; on-device fetch blocked (proxy 403).

publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City
title: Is the U.S. Labor Force Nearing Its Peak?
key_claim: The US labour force declined in 2025 and is likely nearing its peak; CBO projects net immigration falling from above 3.5 million in 2023 to 574,000 in 2026.
frame_summary: Argues the labour force's long expansion is ending because immigration and participation gains can no longer offset ageing, so supply, not demand, will increasingly cap employment growth.
verbatim_quote: After peaking above 3.5 million in 2023, the CBO projects net immigration will fall to 574,000 in 2026.
verbatim_list: The purple bars in Chart 3 show that the labor force declined last year.
If there had been no immigration from 2018 to 2025 (second bar), the labor force would have increased by less than 2 million
notes: Structural anchor (3-6 month band): the canonical regional-Fed statement of the labour-supply ceiling. Confirmed by web fetch 10 October 2026; on-device fetch blocked (proxy 403).

title: What low breakeven employment growth means for the US labour market
key_claim: Oxford Economics forecasts the US breakeven pace of monthly employment growth falling from 50,000 today to zero next year and potentially slightly negative by 2028.
frame_summary: Argues restrictive immigration and demographic shifts are lowering the job growth needed to hold unemployment steady, so weak payroll numbers carry a different meaning than before.
verbatim_quote: the breakeven pace of monthly employment growth forecasted to decline from 50,000 today to zero next year
verbatim_list: restrictive immigration policies and demographic shifts are contributing to a lower breakeven rate
notes: Consultancy briefing; full report is behind a form, the summary page is public. Confirmed by web fetch 10 October 2026.

title: Tracking the Impact of AI on the Labor Market
key_claim: Measures of AI usage show no connection to changes in US employment or unemployment, and the occupational mix is not yet changing in line with AI adoption (updated 15 September 2026).
frame_summary: Argues the aggregate data do not yet show an AI footprint in employment, so attributing weak hiring to AI is not supported by the tracker.
verbatim_quote: Measures of AI usage show no connection to changes in employment or unemployment
verbatim_list: The occupational mix is not yet changing in ways that clearly align with the introduction of AI into the workforce.
notes: Academic policy lab tracker; page also states 'Updated: September 15, 2026'. Confirmed by web fetch 10 October 2026.

title: How Did the Post-Pandemic Migration Surge Affect Labor and Housing Markets? (BPEA conference draft)
key_claim: The 2021-2024 migration surge boosted employment by about 0.4 jobs for each surge migrant, with the largest gains in leisure and hospitality and professional and business services.
frame_summary: Argues immigration adds to labour demand as well as supply, so changes in migration move job counts as well as the pool of workers.
verbatim_quote: This 2021-2024 migration surge boosted employment by about 0.4 jobs for each surge migrant
verbatim_list: The increase in employment was largest in the leisure and hospitality and professional and business services sectors.
notes: Brookings Papers on Economic Activity conference draft (preliminary). Date is the conference date on the title page. Confirmed by web fetch 10 October 2026.

title: The labor market could become so backward that the economy will have to shed jobs to keep unemployment steady
key_claim: Oxford Economics puts the breakeven rate at about 50,000 new jobs per month, down from more than 200,000 in 2022 and 2023 when immigration surged.
frame_summary: Frames falling breakeven hiring as a demographic and immigration story in which the economy could eventually need to shed jobs to hold unemployment steady.
verbatim_quote: down from more than 200,000 in 2022 and 2023, when immigration surged.
verbatim_list: the breakeven rate is currently about 50,000 new jobs per month
notes: Tier 3 corroboration of the Oxford Economics estimate; supplies the 2022-2023 comparison. Confirmed by web fetch 10 October 2026.
